direction: Human-paced version with contrast between hook, explanation, caveat, and closing line. Keep it trustworthy and lightly warm, not dramatic.

segments.label: hook
segments.text: If mortgage rates are falling, your payment should fall too, right?

segments.label: setup
segments.text: That is the part catching a lot of people off guard. The renewal trap is simple.

segments.label: mechanism
segments.text: Your new mortgage payment is not compared with the highest rate you saw on the news last year. It is compared with the rate you locked in years ago.

segments.label: contradiction
segments.text: So if you bought or renewed when money was unusually cheap, today's rate can be lower than the peak, but still much higher than your old deal.

segments.label: analogy
segments.text: Think of it like reaching a toll booth. The road ahead may be cheaper than last month, but still more expensive than the road you were already on.

segments.label: stakes
segments.text: That is why this mortgage renewal wave matters. For many households, the problem is not a dramatic crash. It is a slow squeeze.

segments.label: consequence
segments.text: A few hundred dollars more each month. Less room for savings. Less room for mistakes.

segments.label: caveat
segments.text: To be fair, not every borrower is hit the same way. Some renewals will be manageable. Some could even improve.

segments.label: risk
segments.text: The pressure is strongest when the old rate was very low, the mortgage is large, and the budget was already tight.

segments.label: question
segments.text: So the practical question is not just, where will rates go?

segments.label: better_question
segments.text: The better question is, what payment can my budget survive if the headline is wrong?

segments.label: close
segments.text: Because the dangerous mortgage payment is not always the biggest one. It is the one you planned for too late.
